cards.explanation: The answer is to be confident and unashamed before Him. The writer says to remain in Christ "…so that when He appears, we may be confident and unashamed before Him at His coming." Notice he doesn't say nervous, and he doesn't say hiding behind the couch. I think he wants them walking up with their heads up.

The answer is True. The writer says, "If you know that He is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him." So if somebody is practicing righteousness, the text says they've been born of Him. Simple as dough, flour and a little water.

The answer is children of God, friends! The writer says, "Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God." Look at the word "given." The Father's love is what He has given. My cookie cutter kids called me Papa, but this is a way bigger deal.

The answer is False. The text says we should be called children of God, and then adds, "And that is what we are!" So it's not only a title. Then he says it again in verse 2: "…we are now children of God…" He says it twice, so I'm guessing he wants it to stick.

The answer is that the world did not know Him. The writer says, "The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him." Think about it like this, friends: if you never met somebody, you won't recognize his kids at the grocery store. The world's trouble starts with not knowing Him, and that's why it doesn't know us.

The answer is like Him! The writer says, "We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him…" That's the part that's still ahead. Right now the writer says we are children of God, and what we will be "…has not yet been revealed." But he knows this much, and he says it plain.

The answer is that they will see Him as He is. The writer says, "…we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is." The word "for" is the reason right there in the verse, friends. Seeing Him as He is comes with being like Him.

The answer is pure. The writer says everyone who has this hope "…purifies himself, just as Christ is pure." Christ is the standard, friends, not the neighbor down the street. And the hope is what he points to right before it, that we will be like Him.
The answer is that he practices lawlessness as well. The writer says, "Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well." Plain, no sugar on it. He doesn't tiptoe, and neither will I.
The answer is sins. The writer says, "…Christ appeared to take away sins…" Not just to point at them or to make a list, friends. To take them away.

The answer is True, and the writer says it right after the other part. "…you know that Christ appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin." Not a speck. Those two things sit side by side in the same verse.

The answer is that he has not seen or known Christ. The writer says, "No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him." It's a serious line, so I'll say it plain and leave it there. It follows right after, "No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning."

The answer is False. The writer warns, "…let no one deceive you: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous." The righteous one is the one who practices it. A claim by itself isn't what he points to.

The answer is True, and I love this verse. The writer says, "This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil." It tells us why the Son of God was revealed, friends. That's what He came to do.

The answer is that God's seed lives in him. The writer says, "…God’s seed abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God." So it's tied to being born of God. The seed abiding in him is the reason the verse gives.

The answer is that he does not love his brother. The writer says, "Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother." So he gives two signs of someone who is not of God, friends. Not practicing righteousness is the first, and not loving his brother is the other.
